passage:
Hrithik, two, bumped his head on the table and wailed.
"Aa ja, beta," called Dadi, arms out.
"I've got him," said Chachi, scooping him up. "Oof, big bump."
Hrithik cried louder, then reached for his cousin. "Tenzin!"
Tenzin, eight, made a funny face. "Look, a fish!"
Hrithik hiccuped, then giggled.
Dadi laughed. "Whoever is closest wins."
He fell asleep on Chachi's shoulder, one fist holding Tenzin's shirt.

qa.q: Who scooped Hrithik up first?
qa.a: Chachi scooped him up.

qa.q: How did Hrithik seem to feel when Tenzin made a funny face?
qa.a: He seemed comforted and safe, stopping crying and giggling.

qa.q: What does this home do well when Hrithik cries?
qa.a: Whoever is nearest comforts him, so he has many familiar people to feel safe with.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel when Hrithik reaches for him?
qa.a: Tenzin probably feels proud and loved, being trusted to cheer up his little cousin.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler in a joint household who is soothed by whoever is nearest and feels safe with many familiar faces.

passage:
Creche note, Tuesday.
At drop-off Kunal clung to his mother Dolma's neck. When she left, he screamed and stood at the door, palms flat on the glass. Other adults' arms did not help. He took my hand only after twenty minutes, still sniffing. When Dolma came back, he ran and buried his face. I suggested she stay five minutes tomorrow and wave clearly before leaving.

qa.q: Where did Kunal stand after his mother left?
qa.a: He stood at the door, palms flat on the glass.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Dolma left the creche?
qa.a: He was very distressed and frightened, screaming and pressing against the glass.

qa.q: What did the carer suggest for tomorrow, and why might it help?
qa.a: That Dolma stay five minutes and wave clearly, so Kunal can settle and know she is going and will come back.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel at drop-off?
qa.a: She probably feels torn and sad leaving him crying, and relieved when he runs to her.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler closely tied to one parent who shows sharp distress when she leaves.

passage: At the community centre's summer camp, Omkar, five, and his cousin Preeti sat together at lunch. Omkar broke his paratha and put half on Preeti's plate without a word. She gave him her banana. Then they both grabbed the red crayon. "Mine!" "No, mine!" Preeti pushed; Omkar cried. The teacher waited. Two minutes later, Omkar held out the crayon. "You do the sun, I do the car." Preeti nodded. By afternoon nap, they lay on one mat, feet touching.

qa.q: What did Omkar put on Preeti's plate?
qa.a: Half of his paratha.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he held out the crayon?
qa.a: He seemed ready to make up, no longer upset, wanting to play together again.

qa.q: Why did the teacher's choice to wait work well?
qa.a: It let the cousins fight and make up on their own, which they do quickly.

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti to share everything with Omkar?
qa.a: It probably feels natural and safe; sharing food and a mat is just normal for her.

grounding: It illustrates a child among cousins who shares without being asked, fights and makes up quickly.

passage: Avni, you're crying because your mother said your cousin got better marks? Come, sit near your Dolma Ama. When I was a girl of ten, in our big house in Kalimpong, there were nine of us cousins. My cousin Pema was the clever one. Every night at dinner, my uncle said, "Pema came first. What about you, Dolma?" I would push my momos around the plate. Some days it made me study harder, I won't lie. I stayed up with a candle. But mostly I felt I was never enough, whatever I did. One day I came second in the district drawing contest. My uncle asked if Pema had entered. I tore up the certificate. Then Pema found the pieces, stuck them together and put it on her wall. "You draw better than me," she said. I never forgot that.

qa.q: What did Dolma come second in?
qa.a: The district drawing contest.

qa.q: How did young Dolma feel at dinner when her uncle compared her with Pema?
qa.a: She felt hurt and not good enough, pushing her momos around, even if it sometimes made her study harder.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dolma Ama's story?
qa.a: Pema sticking the torn certificate together and saying Dolma drew better, which showed Dolma her own worth apart from the comparison.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt being the one everyone praised?
qa.a: Pema might have felt uncomfortable being used to measure Dolma, and caring enough to show she admired Dolma's drawing.

grounding: It illustrates a child compared to a cousin who feels both motivated and hurt, and a quiet sense of never being enough.

passage: Last winter I noticed something that still makes me smile. I am Dilnaz, Mamaiji, grandmother of four, and I live with my son's family in Mumbai. Every morning I tie my kusti and say my prayers by the window. One day my granddaughter Kavitha, nine, stood beside me with a ribbon round her waist, moving her lips like me. Her mother is a Hindu from Pune, and Kavitha goes to the temple with her too. But she had learnt my words, just by watching. Later she scolded her brother with my saying: "Good thoughts, good words, good deeds, Rustom!" I laughed so hard. My friends in small flats have to phone their grandchildren. Mine hear me every day. I felt useful again.

qa.q: What did Kavitha tie round her waist?
qa.a: A ribbon.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel on seeing Kavitha copy her prayers?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt delighted and useful again, as if her role had meaning.

qa.q: What does living together give this family that others may have to seek out?
qa.a: Daily contact lets Kavitha pick up Dilnaz's prayers and sayings naturally, while grandparents in separate homes may need phone calls or planned visits.

qa.q: How might Kavitha see her grandmother's morning prayers?
qa.a: Kavitha probably finds them interesting and special, a part of her day she wants to join in, alongside the temple visits with her mother.

grounding: It illustrates a grandmother who notices a grandchild copying her prayers and sayings and feels her role has meaning.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10.
Yamini came in after her class teacher mentioned she had been sleeping in lessons. She lives with eleven family members in a three-room flat in Jaipur. She shares a room with two cousins and her grandmother. She said she tries to call her friend Zainab at night, but "someone is always listening, or asking who it is." Last week she slammed the bathroom door so hard the latch broke, and was scolded for being selfish. She said, crying, "I love them. I just want one door that closes."
I told her wanting privacy is normal and not selfish. We practised a calm way to ask: one hour on Sundays in the terrace room, phone calls on the walk home. She raised it with her mother that evening. Her mother agreed to the terrace hour. I will check in next week.

qa.q: How many family members does Yamini live with?
qa.a: Eleven family members, in a three-room flat in Jaipur.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when she said "I just want one door that closes"?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and guilty, loving her family but craving privacy and feeling selfish for wanting it.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Yamini do instead of slamming doors?
qa.a: Practise a calm, specific request, like a terrace hour on Sundays, so her need for space could be asked for kindly.

qa.q: How might Yamini's mother see the request for a terrace hour?
qa.a: She may have been surprised but understanding, agreeing once it was asked for calmly rather than through slammed doors.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager in a crowded joint home who craves privacy, feels selfish for it, and shows it by slamming doors until she learns to ask.

passage:
June: Shalini, fourteen, let herself into the silent Gurgaon flat at 3:30. Both parents worked till eight. She could eat what she liked and watch anything. The first week it felt like freedom. By the third, she was scrolling for five hours straight, eating chips for lunch, the TV on just for the noise.
July: One afternoon the power went out. The quiet pressed on her ears. She realised she hadn't spoken aloud all day. She messaged Mummy, "When are you home?" and felt stupid when Mummy said, "Usual time, beta."
August: Amandeep aunty from the flat below, a retired teacher, knocked with a bowl of kadhi. "I'm alone too. Come for tea tomorrow?" Shalini went. Now Tuesdays and Fridays she does homework at Amandeep aunty's table, arguing about cricket. The phone still fills the other days, but less.

qa.q: What time did Shalini's parents work till?
qa.a: Both parents worked till eight.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when the power went out in July?
qa.a: She felt lonely, the quiet pressing on her ears, realising she hadn't spoken aloud all day.

qa.q: What helped Shalini, and why?
qa.a: Amandeep aunty's invitation gave her regular company twice a week, filling some of the gap that screens had been filling.

qa.q: How might Amandeep aunty feel about Shalini's visits?
qa.a: She probably feels glad and less lonely too, since she said she was alone and enjoys the cricket arguments.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager in a small nuclear family who feels both freedom and loneliness after school, with screens filling the gap.

passage:
In the admissions office of the Kolkata college, Arnab's phone buzzed nonstop. The family group had forty messages. Mejo kaka: "Geology? What job?" Mama: "Engineering is safe." Pishi: "Ask Arnab what he wants!" Arnab, nineteen, sat opposite the counsellor, Mr Karthik, feeling his chest tighten. He had not even filled the form yet and the family had decided.
"Everything alright?" Karthik asked.
"My uncles," Arnab said. "They care. But it's my life."
Karthik smiled. "Both can be true. What would you tell them?"
Arnab thought, then typed: "Thank you all for thinking of me. I've listened, and I'll call Mama tonight to talk it through. But I'm choosing geology. I love it." He pressed send before he could change his mind. Pishi replied first: a thumbs up. Then Mama: "Call tonight." Arnab filled the form.

qa.q: Which relative asked the family to ask Arnab what he wants?
qa.a: Pishi.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when he saw the family messages?
qa.a: Arnab felt pressured and cared for at once, his chest tightening because the family seemed to have decided for him.

qa.q: What made Arnab's message a wise reply?
qa.a: It thanked the family, promised to listen, and still clearly owned the final choice of geology.

qa.q: How might Mama see Arnab's message?
qa.a: Mama may be worried about job safety but willing to talk, replying "Call tonight" rather than refusing.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult whose course choice is discussed by uncles and aunts, and who thanks them, listens and still owns the decision.

passage:
My dear Sarita,
You told us last night that you and Rohit want your own flat after the wedding, in the new building near your office. I didn't say much. Your mother thought I was angry. I wasn't. I was sad, and I want to be honest with you.
I grew up with twenty-two people under one roof in Bareilly. My brothers left one by one, and each time I felt the house shrink. Now you. I lay awake thinking the family I knew is ending.
But this morning I watched you make tea for your Dadi, as you do every day, and I thought: kindness doesn't need one roof. So here is what I ask, not demand. Sunday lunch with us, as often as you can. Festivals together. Call your Dadi. The rest is yours to shape.
With love,
Papa (Ujjwal)

qa.q: Where did Papa grow up?
qa.a: In Bareilly, with twenty-two people under one roof.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Sarita announced the new flat?
qa.a: He felt sad and lay awake, feeling that the family he knew was ending.

qa.q: What does Papa ask for, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sunday lunches, festivals together and calls to Dadi, asked for rather than demanded, which accepts the new household while keeping closeness through kindness.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sarita would probably feel relieved and loved, knowing her father accepts her choice and only asks for regular time together.

grounding: It illustrates an elder who sees his child wanting a smaller household, feels the joint family slipping, and accepts it while asking for gatherings.

passage:
"Ammi, can we talk before dinner?"
Sharmila looked up from the dough. "Your face says something big."
Imran sat on the kitchen stool. "I've found a flat. Near the office. One bedroom."
Her hands stopped. "You're leaving us?"
"No. I'm moving. That's different." His voice shook. "I've been scared to say it for months. I don't want you to think I'm abandoning you and Abbu."
"People will say our son left his parents."
"People will also see me here every Friday for dinner. And Sunday I'll take Abbu to his check-up, like always. I'll keep a key. If anything happens at night, I'm fifteen minutes away."
She kneaded in silence. "Fridays. Every Friday."
"Every Friday. And you'll come see the flat first?"
Sharmila sighed, then smiled a little. "Someone has to check you're buying proper vegetables."

qa.q: How far away will Imran's flat be?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes away.

qa.q: How did Imran feel before telling his mother, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt guilty and scared, his voice shaking and admitting he had been afraid to say it for months.

qa.q: Why did Imran's approach ease the shift?
qa.a: He talked honestly and offered concrete plans for visits and duties, like Friday dinners and Abbu's check-ups, instead of a sudden announcement.

qa.q: How did Sharmila's feelings change during the talk?
qa.a: She was shocked and worried about what people would say, then softened into a small smile once she heard the plans for Fridays.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult moving out who fears seeming to abandon parents, and eases it with honest talk about visits and duties.
